explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Jonathan is named right there, along with his brothers Abinadab and Malchishua. The verse says the Philistines “killed Saul’s sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua.” (1 Chronicles 10:2) Saul was Israel's king, so this lands on his whole family. I think this is a quiet, hard line to read.

Close, but the text says otherwise. The verse says the Philistines “killed Saul’s sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua.” (1 Chronicles 10:2) So Jonathan is right there in the list. Saul was Israel's king, and his sons were with him in this fight. It's a heavy line, friend.

explanations.answer: Run him through with a sword
explanations.explanation: That's what he asks. Saul tells him, “Draw your sword and run me through with it…” (1 Chronicles 10:4) The archers have already wounded him, and the Philistines are closing in. This is a very heavy moment, friend, so I'll just say it plainly.

explanations.answer: Carry him down off the mountain
explanations.explanation: That's a kind thought, but it isn't what Saul asks. He says, “Draw your sword and run me through with it…” (1 Chronicles 10:4) Nothing in the verse mentions carrying him anywhere. The battle is on Mount Gilboa, and the archers have already wounded him. It's a hard scene, friend.

explanations.answer: Hold off the archers for him
explanations.explanation: Not this time. The archers have already overtaken Saul and wounded him by the time he speaks. (1 Chronicles 10:3) What he asks of his armor-bearer is to “Draw your sword and run me through with it…” (1 Chronicles 10:4) The request has nothing to do with holding anyone off.

Yes, that's the word Saul uses. He says the “uncircumcised men will come and torture me!” (1 Chronicles 10:4) That's what he's afraid of as the Philistines close in. I think that tells us how scared he is. It's a heavy verse, friend.

Ransom is a fair guess, since you pay it to get a person back. But Saul never says that word. He says the “uncircumcised men will come and torture me!” (1 Chronicles 10:4) So the fear he names is torture, not a price to be paid.

Enslaving is a hard word, but Saul doesn't use it. His words are, “…these uncircumcised men will come and torture me!” (1 Chronicles 10:4) Torture is what he says he's afraid of. It's a heavy moment, friend.

It goes the other way, friend. The armor-bearer “was terrified and refused to do it.” (1 Chronicles 10:4) Saul had asked him to draw his sword, and he wouldn't. After that, Saul takes his own sword. It's a heavy part of the story.

That's right. The text says the armor-bearer “was terrified and refused to do it.” (1 Chronicles 10:4) Saul asked, and he would not. Then Saul took his own sword. This is one of the heaviest spots in the passage, friend.

explanations.answer: He falls on his own sword too
explanations.explanation: Yes. The verse says that when he “saw that Saul was dead, he too fell on his own sword and died.” (1 Chronicles 10:5) The text doesn't tell us what he was thinking, so I won't guess. I'll just say it's a sad line, friend. Chronicles reports it and moves on.

explanations.answer: He hides Saul's body in a cave
explanations.explanation: No cave in this story. The armor-bearer “fell on his own sword and died.” (1 Chronicles 10:5) And the next day the Philistines find Saul and his sons on Mount Gilboa, right where they fell. (1 Chronicles 10:8) Nobody hid anything.

explanations.answer: He runs to warn Saul's household
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't send him anywhere. When he sees Saul is dead, he “too fell on his own sword and died.” (1 Chronicles 10:5) So there's no running and no warning in this verse. It's a heavy one, friend.

explanations.answer: They abandon their cities and run
explanations.explanation: That's what they do. The Israelites in the valley saw the army had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, so they “abandoned their cities and ran away.” (1 Chronicles 10:7) The whole country is shaken, friend. With the king gone, nobody stays.

explanations.answer: They gather to fight the Philistines
explanations.explanation: That would take some nerve, but the text goes the other way. The Israelites in the valley saw the army had fled, and they “abandoned their cities and ran away.” (1 Chronicles 10:7) Nobody is said to gather for another fight here. The Philistines walk in after they leave.

explanations.answer: They send to Judah for help
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the verse mentions sending for help. What it says is that they “abandoned their cities and ran away.” (1 Chronicles 10:7) Then the Philistines came to their cities. It all happened fast, friend.

Yes, that's the word. The verse says the Philistines “came and occupied their cities.” (1 Chronicles 10:7) The Israelites ran, and the Philistines moved right into the empty towns. That's a big loss for Israel, friend.

Burning is a natural guess, but the verse doesn't mention fire. It says the Philistines “came and occupied their cities.” (1 Chronicles 10:7) The cities were left empty, and the Philistines moved in. They took over the places and didn't burn them.

Close in spirit, but the verse doesn't mention any tearing down. It says the Philistines “came and occupied their cities.” (1 Chronicles 10:7) So the towns were taken over, not knocked flat. The Israelites had left, and the Philistines moved in.

They did the opposite, friend. The Philistines “sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines to proclaim the news in the temple of their idols and among their people.” (1 Chronicles 10:9) They wanted it known everywhere. The news went to the temples and to the people.

That's right. The Philistines “sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines to proclaim the news in the temple of their idols and among their people.” (1 Chronicles 10:9) The news went out across their whole land. They kept nothing quiet.

explanations.answer: They bring back the bodies of Saul and his sons
explanations.explanation: Yes. All their men of valor “set out and retrieved the bodies of Saul and his sons and brought them to Jabesh.” (1 Chronicles 10:12) Jabesh-gilead was a town in Israel. They heard what had been done, and they went and got the bodies. I think that's a brave and kind thing to do, friend.

explanations.answer: They attack the temple of the Philistine gods
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't send them to fight at the temple. It says their men of valor “set out and retrieved the bodies of Saul and his sons and brought them to Jabesh.” (1 Chronicles 10:12) Jabesh-gilead was a town in Israel. Their job was getting the bodies home.

explanations.answer: They send gifts to buy back the bodies
explanations.explanation: No gifts are mentioned. Their men of valor “set out and retrieved the bodies of Saul and his sons and brought them to Jabesh.” (1 Chronicles 10:12) Jabesh-gilead was a town in Israel. The text says they went themselves, and it says nothing of buying anything.

Yes, that's it. The men of Jabesh “buried their bones under the oak in Jabesh and fasted seven days.” (1 Chronicles 10:12) Fasting means going without food, so they stopped eating for that stretch. I think that shows how deeply they grieved. It's a quiet, faithful ending to a rough scene, friend.

No party at Jabesh. The text says they “buried their bones under the oak in Jabesh and fasted seven days.” (1 Chronicles 10:12) Fasting means going without food, and that's the opposite of a feast. I think this was a time of mourning, friend.

The text has them staying put. They “buried their bones under the oak in Jabesh and fasted seven days.” (1 Chronicles 10:12) Nobody is said to march anywhere. Fasting means going without food for those seven days.

explanations.answer: He was unfaithful to the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes, and Chronicles says it outright. “So Saul died for his unfaithfulness to the LORD…” (1 Chronicles 10:13) The writer names it directly, so there's no guessing. After all the battle, we get the reason, friend.

explanations.answer: He lost his courage in battle
explanations.explanation: That's a natural guess after a battle like this. But the writer gives a different reason. “So Saul died for his unfaithfulness to the LORD…” (1 Chronicles 10:13) The text points to his unfaithfulness, not to courage in the fight.

explanations.answer: He grew proud of his power
explanations.explanation: Pride isn't the reason Chronicles gives. It says, “So Saul died for his unfaithfulness to the LORD, because he did not keep the word of the LORD…” (1 Chronicles 10:13) Here the writer names unfaithfulness. He goes on to say Saul didn't keep the LORD's word.

Yes. The writer says Saul “even consulted a medium for guidance…” (1 Chronicles 10:13) That's one of the reasons given for his unfaithfulness. A medium is someone who claims to speak with the dead. The verse goes on to say he didn't inquire of the LORD.

The text says it did happen. Saul “even consulted a medium for guidance…” (1 Chronicles 10:13) A medium is someone who claims to speak with the dead. That's part of the reason Chronicles gives for his death. The verse goes on to say he didn't inquire of the LORD.

Yes. The LORD “turned the kingdom over to David son of Jesse.” (1 Chronicles 10:14) So the kingdom doesn't just float off into the air, friend. The writer says it goes to David. Saul's story closes, and David's is coming.
Abner was Saul's army commander (1 Samuel 14:50), so I see why his name came to mind. But this verse names someone else. The LORD “turned the kingdom over to David son of Jesse.” (1 Chronicles 10:14)

Joab was over David's army (2 Samuel 8:16), so he's close to the story. But he isn't who this verse names. The LORD “turned the kingdom over to David son of Jesse.” (1 Chronicles 10:14) Joab served under the man who got the kingdom.
